newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: News re-rated on relief at U.S. TV deals.
newsitem.headline: News re-rated on relief at U.S. TV deals.

text.p: News Corp Ltd's shares roared back into favour on Thursday as investors and analysts re-rated the global media group's prospects after it announced two deals to buy and sell U.S. television assets worth US$3 billion.
News' shares surged as much as 38 cents or 6.5 percent to a new three month high of A$6.25 in hectic morning trade.

Analysts and brokers welcomed News' decision to sell U.S. ASkyB satellite assets to the Primestar group of pay television operators for US$1.1 billion, saying it had removed the risk of News having to plough more money into the new infrastructure.
The Primestar deal comes as a relief given that News Corp has sunk considerable funds into ASkyB," said Bob Peters, media analyst at ANZ Investments.
"The Primestar deal takes out what essentially could have been a very big black hole for News Corp," added Vince Pepe, media analyst at ABN-Amro Hoare Govett.
News Corp executive chairman Rupert Murdoch was effectively monetarising his investment in ASkyB, said HSBC James Capel broker Neil Franklin.
The News and MCI Communications Corp ASkyB joint venture will receive US$1.1 billion of Primestar non-voting stock and notes in return for the satellite assets.

News' US$1.9 billion purchase of International Family Entertainment Inc, which runs family and children's cable television channels, was also welcomed because it was bought for cash rather than with News' non-voting preferred shares. The preferred stock rose up to 47 cents to A$5.28.
News' use of the preferred shares to buy marketing company Heritage Media Corp in March was savaged by investors worried about dilution and perceptions of an uncontrolled expansion.
"These deals will be a very big positive for News, firstly because they haven't used DPs (preferred shares) and they've conserved their cash," Pepe said.
"The main factor driving the stock is that there's no DP issuance," said HSBC James Capel broker Neil Franklin.

News' March 17 announcement of the Heritage deal, which involves issuing US$754 million of preferred shares and assuming US$600 million in debt, sparked a 18 percent-three month slide in News' preferred share price to a 15-month low.
The slide hurt investors even more because it was set against a ten percent rally in the Australian All Ordinaries index between March and mid-June.
"It's a brief ray of sunshine between clouds," Franklin said.

Most analysts and brokers said they were unconcerned with the apparently high price paid by News' unit Fox Kids Worldwide for IFE, pointing to what appeared a strong fit between Fox Kids and IFE's children and family channels.

tandard and Poor's Corp put News' BBB credit rating on negative CreditWatch after the two deals, saying the price paid represented a very high multiple and that the venture would not be able to generate net cash flow given the expected debt financing involved.
Some analysts said the US$1.9 billion price represented an earnings before tax, interest depreciation and abnormals (EBITDA) multiple of about 17.5 times.

Analysts said this appeared high, but was acceptable in the restricted world of U.S. cable tv where new competition was limited because all existing cable space was filled and strong brand names were difficult to create amid a barrage of channels.
Digital television, which could open up space on the spectrum, was still some years away in the United States.
"If you have an established franchise, that's extremely valuable in the short to medium term," said ANZ's Peters.
IFE's Family Channel reaches about 69 million households in the United States.
-- Sydney Newsroom 61-2 9373-1800
